newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fighting and diplomacy ahead of Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Fighting and diplomacy ahead of Zaire talks.

text.p: South Africa and Zaire's civil war rivals prepared for Wednesday's shipboard summit with host Nelson Mandela saying a peaceful settlement was still possible.
But rebel leader Laurent Kabila told a U.S. radio station that Wednesday was veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko's last chance to hand over power peacefully.
Both Zaire's government and residents in contact by radio with the capital Kinshasa reported fighting on the road to the city.
"I am very confident that we will make progress...as long as everybody understands that this is not an event, it is a process," Mandela told reporters in Cape Town on Tuesday.
Kabila told California-based Pacifica Radio on Monday that a peaceful transfer of power depended on Mobutu, who seized power in Africa's third largest nation in 1965.
"Mobutu has to go, to relinquish power to the alliance, that is on Wednesday, the day after tomorrow," he said.
Reports reaching Kinshasa said the rebels had taken the key bridge over the River Kwango and Zaire's armed forces (FAZ) had pulled back to Mbankana about 150 km (100 miles) from the city.

Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba told Reuters he could make no immediate comment on the reports. On Monday, he told reporters there was fierce fighting in the region of Kenge, 60 km (40 miles) to the east of the bridge.
Mobutu, 66, is fighting cancer and Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, control three-quarters of Zaire.
"The end should come very swiftly. I do not see the hold-out on Kinshasa lasting long. It will come in the next few days," Kabila's son Joseph, a frontline commander, said on Monday.

Mandela is scheduled to host direct talks between Mobutu and Kabila aboard the South African ice-breaker Outeniqua in or near the Congolese port of Pointe Noire on Wednesday. A first meeting on the ship on May 4 ended inconclusively.
Mandela said he had spoken regularly in the past few days to both men and the leaders of countries such as Burkina Faso, Togo and Nigeria in a bid to map out a settlement.
Aides to South Africa's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki, said he planned to travel to Zaire for pre-summit talks with both Mobutu and Kabila.
"We are all on standby to go. The deputy president wants to make sure that there is some agreement in place before they go onto the ship tomorrow," Ricky Naidoo, his spokesman, said.

Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga, told Belgian RTL-TVI television on Monday his father was ready to make serious concessions, but he declined to go into detail. "Everything depends on the negotiations." he said.

Kabila said on Monday his alliance would not accept any kind of transition government suggested by Western powers or other mediators. "They are trying to complicate by machination, intrigue, so that the Mobutists, the ones who have destroyed this country, remain in power without their boss Mobutu," he said.
